Learn to cook. Trust me, living off frozen food gets old real quick.

Yup, it took me too long to realize how important this is. I have a rice cooker and a large frying pan that makes me just about anything I want. I pretty much just season beef or chicken differently every time I cook so it never gets old. Kind of funny how many different "laws of three" or "rules of thirds" there are. I guess three is just a convenient number. In survival it's the rule of thumb that you can survive three minutes without air, three hours without shelter, three days without water, and three weeks without food. Some people add "three seconds without hope" on there. Then there's the rule of thirds in SCUBA diving that basically states you should use one third of your gas on the first half of the dive, one third on the second half, and leave the final third unused as a reserve.

Now I have another law of threes to add to my collection.

It really depends on your situation. You're moving out.

  • Where are you moving in? Your own house? An apartment? Solo? Roommates?

  • What's your financial situation? Do you have a job lined up? Student?

If you're moving out for school into a dorm, a lot of things will likely be provided for you. At least at my dorm, we had a meal plan so cooking wasn't necessary. Apart from the obvious, I found it handy to have a basic tool kit at school. We did a lot of projects (engineering school) and it's nice to have the basics on hand to fix things (like your computers) as well. Just make sure you adapt to school life away from home, you may want to set alarms to make sure you're up and ready for class until you adjust to your schedule.

If you're moving out on your own to start your career, you'll need to bring everything as you'll be starting from nothing. Hopefully you have some money saved to buy some basic furniture for your new place and some kitchen and cleaning supplies. Make sure you set up your utilities (including Internet and phone/cable, if you use them) before you move in so you can have your installation appointment as soon as possible. Open a bank account once you get to the new area (if moving out of town) and transfer any money you have into it, then set up direct deposit if you can. If you're not living paycheck-to-paycheck, go ahead and sign up for a credit card and auto-pay any bills you can to it, then either set up auto pay for your credit card bill or sign up for email reminders and pay as soon as you get them. That way you'll rack up rewards on your credit card while ensuring all your bills get paid on time. Don't overspend, especially when you're just starting out. Pay your bills and save most of the rest. Then in a year or two you'll have a nice savings reserve. Also, if your employer offers it, sign up for your retirement plan as soon as possible and maximize contribution if you can. It's best to start that when you're young.

Oh man. Okay, this is easy. Other people have said some stuff that I'm gonna elaborate on.

Buy a plunger. This is paramount. Not tomorrow. Today. Before you move out. Stop reading and go buy a fucking plunger.

I'm going to assume you're not broke broke, but you won't have tons of expendable income. Utilities are first, food is second, laundry third, and what's left over is spending money. Just fuckin with you, you don't have spending money. Repeat that. no matter how much you have, you don't have spending money. not yet. Not for games, not for energy drinks, not for fast food. If you want to go out with friends, you're not going to be able to buy almost anything else that's not necessary. You may see your paychecks, and say, "Well, my bills all come out to $XXXX.XX a month, and my checks come out to $XXXX + $YYY, I can buy that thing that costs $ZZ!"

You're wrong. The reason is because you don't have those checks yet. Crucial mistake; plotting for your future income. If you live as if every dollar you have is the last one you'll receive, you won't ever spend more than you need. I'm sick of seeing people my age (almost 30) who are absolutely fucked if they have to spend more than they make on one paycheck at one time. If you have a kid, or have other incidentals that sap your income, I feel for you. But no normal, youngish person with no kids, illnesses or convictions should be having to choose between a car repair or rent if they've got a job that gives them more than 30 hours a week.

Car repair reminds me of another thing, the toilet paper sale. It's hard for a lot of young people to realize long term cost and the effects of it. They will by shit they can't afford on credit cause it's "only" $35 a month, even though the $200 couch they finance through rent-a-center ends up costing them $4,000 over the lease term. Or that they buy the 4 pack of TP for $3.99 "on sale" every week instead of the 25 pack for $16.99 because they would rather spend $3.99 at the checkout line. Every thing you buy, you should think about every part of it. Will you need to replace it? How often? Will it help you make money? Will it cost you more money after you get it home? Is that truck really worth $1,000? Would it be worth $1,000 if you had an itemized list for $12,000 worth of repairs and maintenance over the next 4 years, or should you buy the $3.500 car for $6,000 in maintenance? Are those $30 shoes you wear to work at Pizza Hut really better? Or would the $70 pair that you won't have to replace every 3 months be better?

You spend more money on the shit you need, you'll have less money for the shit you want, for a while. But remember, you don't have spending money yet. Because you're saving it.

A few other key things, don't leave your electronic shit on, and practice being a little hungry and a little uncomfortable with the heat/cold. Don't sweat out a 112 degree summer, but don't crank the AC to 65 for 3 months at a time either. Friends who forget about you when you don't go drinking with them aren't great friends at all.

Get a gym membership. You're here, so I'm gonna assume you're somewhat "nerdy," get a gym membership and get into lifting. Study it. Master it like it's a game. This will help you with your dietary spending, and $30 a month for a membership will pay for itself in less snacks and junk food. Also, fit people get hired easier. It's been studied. Less likely to get fired or evicted too.
